'''Newbury''' is the principal town in the west of the county of Berkshire in the United Kingdom. It is situated on the River Kennet and the Kennet and Avon Canal, and has a town centre containing many seventeenth century buildings.


 Location 
Newbury is situated on the River Kennet, the valley of which forms an important east-west transport route, served by the Kennet and Avon Canal, the Great Western Railway line from London to the West Country and the old A four road from London to Bristol. The latter road has been replaced as a long distance route by the M four motorway which here runs parallel three miles to the north.

At Newbury this east-west route is crossed by an equally important north-south route, from the major south coast port of Southampton to the industrial centres of the Midlands. Although this route was once served by a railway route, today it is only served by the A three four road, which today bypasses Newbury to the west on an alignment partially using the old rail route (see also 'History' below).

The town is surrounded on three sides (north, west and south) by the North Wessex Downs Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and the downland to the south rises steeply out of the river valley giving good views.

The Kennet and Avon Canal runs through the heart of Newbury, Berkshire

'''Nearby towns and cities:''' Thatcham, Hungerford, Didcot, Reading, Oxford, Basingstoke, Winchester

'''Nearby villages:''' Speen, Shaw, Donnington, Bagnor, Greenham, Wash Common, Cold Ash, Chieveley, Highclere, Burghclere, Hermitage, Kintbury, Kingsclere, Lambourn

'''Nearby places of interest:''' Combe Gibbet, Donnington Castle, Sandham Memorial Chapel, Highclere Castle, Watermill Theatre, Watership Down

 History 

Newbury was founded late in the eleventh century and acquired its name through being ''new'' in the sense of postdating the Domesday Survey. Historically, the town's economic foundation was the cloth trade. This is reflected in the person of the fourteenth century cloth magnate Jack O'Newbury and the later tale of the Newbury Coat. The latter was the outcome of a bet as to whether a gentleman's suit could be produced by the end of a day from wool taken from the sheep's back earlier the same day.

Newbury was the site of two English Civil War battles, the First Battle of Newbury in one six four three and the Second Battle of Newbury in one six four four . The nearby Donnington Castle was reduced in the aftermath of the second battle.

In one seven nine five , local magistrates, meeting nearby, introduced the Speenhamland System which tied parish welfare payments to the cost of bread.

Newbury is in the Kennet valley. (As viewed from Donnington Castle)
A large airforce base was established during the Second World War at Greenham Common on the edge of the town. In the one nine five zero s it became home to US Air Force bombers and tankers, for which it was equipped with the longest military runway in the United Kingdom. In the one nine eight zero s it became one of only two bases in the United Kingdom equipped with ground-launched nuclear-armed cruise missiles, causing it to become the site of prolonged and vigorous protests by up to four zero , zero zero zero protesters. With the end of the Cold War the base was closed, the runway was broken up for use as fill material in building the Newbury by-pass (see below), and much of the area restored to heathland.

The town's location at the intersection of the routes from London to Bristol and from Southampton to Birmingham made it, for many years, a transport bottleneck. Since the first bypass opened in one nine six three , the A three four road and M four motorway trunk routes have intersected five km north of the town, at Chieveley. The ring road around the town still suffered serious congestion and the Newbury bypass was proposed in one nine eight one . The plans were approved in one nine nine zero however they were extremely controversial and this led to a major environmentalist campaign (sometimes dubbed the ''Third battle of Newbury'') opposing the development. In spite of this, the road was built and finally opened in one nine nine eight . 

In August two zero zero four , the improved A three four -M four junction was opened which allowed north-south traffic on the A three four to completely bypass the roundabout at the M four .

''See also:'' Newbury Castle, Newbury bypass, Greenham Common, Thatcham

 Economy 

Today, Newbury town has a population of about three two , zero zero zero ( two zero zero four ), and with adjacent towns such as Thatcham is the centre of a continuously built up area with an overall population of around six zero , zero zero zero . 

Newbury is home to the world headquarters of the mobile phone company Vodafone, which is the town's largest employer with four , zero zero zero people. Before building their  one two nine million headquarters in the outskirts of the town in two zero zero three , Vodafone used six four buildings spread across the town centre.

As well as Vodafone Newbury is also home to the UK headquarters of the pharmaceutical company Bayer AG, Newbury Racecourse, a major course on the British horse-racing calendar, Quantel, Stearn Electric, Micro Focus, and Genesys Video Conferencing. It also is home to Newbury Building Society which operates in the local region.

Newbury benefits from good road links, being close to a junction of the M four motorway between London and BristolSouth Wales, and the A three four major road between Southampton and the Midlands. Newbury also has two railway stations, Newbury and Newbury Racecourse on the West of England Main Line line between London and the West Country.

 Sport 
Newbury is home to A.F.C. Newbury, one of only two football clubs sponsored by Vodafone (the other being Manchester United).

Newbury is also home to the rugby union club Newbury R.F.C. (also sponsored by Vodafone). In the two zero zero four zero five season the club finished second in the National Two division earning promotion to National One and is now in the top two six clubs nationally. Newbury had previously won National Four South (now renamed as National Three South) in one nine nine six nine seven with a one zero zero % win record. The club was founded in one nine two eight and moved several years ago to its new ground at Monks Lane which has hosted England U two one fixtures.

It is also home to a major horse-racing fixture, Newbury Racecourse. The most prestigious race in the calendar is the Hennessy Cognac Gold Cup which normally takes place in late November.

 Politics and local government 
Newbury town hall, where the town council meets.
Newbury is a civil parish in its own right, with parish council responsibilities undertaken by '''Newbury Town Council''' (since one nine nine seven ). Newbury is part of, and the administrative centre of, the district administered by the unitary authority of West Berkshire. 

Newbury Town Council currently has two three councillors, representing seven wards of the town. These are Brummel Grove, Clay Hill, Falkland, Northcroft, Pyle Hill, Victoria and St Johns. As of two zero zero five  two zero of the councillors represent the Liberal Democrats whilst three represent the Conservative Party.
 
The reception area in Newbury's library.
Newbury Library, which moved to a new building in July two zero zero zero , provides internet access and a wide range of other services to its users and members.

Newbury is twinned with:
Braunfels in Germany ( one nine six three )
Bagnols-sur-Cze in France ( one nine seven zero )
Eeklo in Belgium ( one nine seven four )
Feltre in Italy ( two zero zero three )

In Parliament, it is in the Newbury constituency. Since the election of May two zero zero five Newbury is represented by Richard Benyon, a Conservative.

Media
Newbury's main weekly newspaper is the Newbury Weekly News, however there are also two free papers available. The Kick FM radio station also broadcasts from Newbury to the local area.

The following local newspapers are distributed in Newbury (circulation in brackets):
 Newbury Weekly News ( two four , three zero zero )
 Newbury & Thatcham Chronicle ( two one , five zero zero )
 Newbury Advertiser & News ( three three , four zero zero )

Education
Newbury has three main secondary schools, St. Bartholomew's School, Park House School and Trinity School, a recent school formed after the closure of Shaw House and Turnpike. There is also Newbury College, a further and higher education college funded by private finance initiative.

Independent schools nearby include Downe House and Cheam.

 A standard convention has been developed to illustrates hands in contract bridge. The cards are shown with each line representing a suit. If the suit is not explicitly indicated by a prefix consisting of symbol describing the suit ( , , , or ) (also abbreviated 'S', 'H', 'D' or 'C' respectively), the order is, from top to bottom, as follows: '''spades''', '''hearts''', '''diamonds''' and '''clubs'''.
Each card in a suit is indicated by its abbreviation. 
 'A', 'K', 'Q', 'J', ' one zero ' (or 'T'), ' nine ', ' eight ', ' seven ', ' six ', ' five ', ' four ', ' three ', ' two '.
Spacing is used for readability only (thus A K J being equal to AKJ).
It is convention to put a card of higher rank always to the left of a card of lower rank, as in the list above. When one hand is ''void'' (i.e. has no cards) in a suit, it is usually denoted by a dash (-). 
The diagram is always drawn with North on top, and other hands as in geographic maps. One or more hands can be left out if irrelevant for presentation. For reader's convenience, in most diagrams South is declarer, so that the reader can see the hand as if (s)he is playing it; exceptions to this rule can occur when reporting deals from actual matches, but even then the players' seats are often rotated to match the common convention.

 The Macintosh II motherboard with its six NuBus slots visible on the left.
Example of a NuBus graphics card, an Apple Display Card two four AC.
'''NuBus''' is a three two -bit parallel computer bus, originally developed at MIT as a part of the '''NuMachine''' workstation project, and eventually used by Apple Computer and NeXT Computer. It is no longer widely used.

NuBus architecture
NuBus was a considerable step forward compared to other interfaces of the day. At the time most computer bus systems were eight -bit, as were the computers they plugged into. However NuBus decided on a three two -bit interface because it was clear the market was headed in this direction.

In addition, NuBus was agnostic about the processor itself. Most buses up to this point were basically the pins on the CPU run out onto the backplane, meaning that the cards had to conform to the signalling and data standards of the machine it was plugged into (being little endian for instance). NuBus made no such assumptions, which meant that a NuBus card could be plugged into any NuBus machine, as long as there was an appropriate device driver.

In order to select the proper device driver, NuBus included an ID scheme that allowed the cards to identify themselves to the host computer during startup. This meant that the user didn't have to configure the system, the bane of bus systems up to that point. For instance, with ISA the driver has to be configured not only for the card, but for any memory it needs, the interrupts it uses, and so on. NuBus required no such configuration, making it one of the first examples of ''plug-and-play'' architecture.

On the downside, while this flexibility made NuBus much simpler for the user and device driver authors, it made things more difficult for the designers of the cards themselves. Whereas most simple bus systems were easily supported with a handful of inputoutput chips designed to be used with that CPU in mind, with NuBus every card and computer had to convert everything in a platform-agnostic NuBus world . Typically this meant adding a NuBus controller chip between the bus and any IO chips on the card, increasing costs. While this is a trivial exercise today, one that all newer buses require, at the time in the one nine eight zero s NuBus was considered complex and expensive.

NuBus implementations
NuMachine was never released, but Texas Instruments later took over the NuBus work in one nine eight zero and standardized it as '''IEEE one one nine six '''. This version used a standard nine six -pin three-row connector, commonly found on other bus systems like VME and PCI, running the system on a one zero MHz clock for a maximum burst throughput of four zero MBs and average speeds of one zero to two zero MBs. A later addition, '''NuBus nine zero ''', bumped the clock rate to two zero MHz for better throughput, burst increasing to about seven zero MBs, and average to about three zero MBs.

NuBus was first used in the Texas Instruments Lisp Machine, the TI Explorer, a derivative of the MIT NuMachine design work. Shortly thereafter, in one nine eight six , Texas Instruments used it in the S one five zero zero multiprocessor UNIX system.

NuBus was later selected by Apple Computer for use in their Macintosh II project, where its plug-n-play nature fit well with the Mac philosophy of ease-of-use. It was used in most of their Mac line through the late one nine eight zero s and into the one nine nine zero s, and was upgraded to NuBus nine zero starting with the Macintosh Quadras. Early Quadras only supported the two zero MHz rate when two cards were talking to each other, since the motherboard controller was not upgraded. This was later addressed in the six six zero AV and eight four zero AV models, and used on the early PowerMac models. Apple's implementation also supplied an always-on + five V trickle power supply for tasks such as watching the phone line while the computer was turned off. This was apparently part of an unapproved NuBus standard.

NuBus was also selected by NeXT Computer for their line of machines, but used a different physical PCB layout. NuBus appears to have seen little use outside these roles, and when Apple switched to PCI in the mid one nine nine zero s, NuBus quickly disappeared.

 '''George Cavendish''' ( one five zero zero c. one five six two ), English writer, the biographer of Cardinal Thomas Wolsey, was the elder son of Thomas Cavendish (died one five two three ), clerk of the pipe in the exchequer, and his wife, Alice Smith of Padbrook Hall. 

Cavendish was the great-grandson of Sir John Cavendish from whom the Dukes of Devonshire and the Dukes of Newcastle inherited the family name of Cavendish. George was an English courtier and author and the brother of William Cavendish, the third husband of Bess of Hardwick. He was probably born at his father's manor of Cavendish, in Suffolk. Later the family
resided in London, in the parish of St Albans, Wood Street, where Thomas Cavendish died in one five two four . Shortly after this event George married Margery Kemp, of Spains Hall, an heiress, and the niece of Sir Thomas More. 

About one five two seven he entered the service of Cardinal Wolsey as gentleman-usher, and for the next three years he was divided from his wife, children and estates, in the closest personal attendance on the great man. Cavendish was wholly devoted to Wolsey's interests, and also he saw in this appointment an opportunity to gratify his master-passion, a craving to see and be acquainted with strangers, in especial with men in honour and authority. He was faithful to his master in disgrace, and showed the courage of the loyal servitor. It is plain that he enjoyed Wolsey's closest confidence to the end, for after the cardinal's death George Cavendish was called before the privy council and closely examined as to Wolsey's latest acts and words. He gave his evidence so clearly and with so much natural dignity, that he won the applause of the hostile council, and the praise of being a just and diligent servant. He was not allowed to suffer in pocket by his fidelity to his master, but retired, as it would seem, a wealthy man to his estate of Glemsford, in West Suffolk, in one five three zero . He was only thirty years of age, but his appetite for being acquainted with strange acts and persons was apparently sated, for we do not hear of his engaging in any more adventures. 

It is not to be doubted that Cavendish had taken down notes of Wolsey's conversation and movements, for many years passed before his biography was composed. At length, in one five five seven , he wrote it out in its final form. It was not, however, possible to publish it in the author's lifetime, but it was widely circulated in MS. Evidently one of these MSS. fell into William Shakespeare's hands, for that poet made use of it in his ''Henry VIII'', although it is excessive to say, as NAME Singer has done, that Shakespeare merely put Cavendish's language into verse. The book was first printed in one six four one , in a garbled text, and under the title of ''The Negotiations of Thomas Wolsey''. The genuine text, from contemporary MSS., was given to the world in one eight one zero , and more fully in one eight one five . Until that time it was believed that the book was the composition of George Cavendish's younger brother William, the founder of Chatsworth House, who also was attached to Wolsey. Joseph Hunter proved this to be impossible, and definitely asserted the claim of George. The latter is believed to have died at Glemsford in or about one five six two .

The intrinsic value of Cavendish's ''Life of Cardinal Wolsey'' has long been perceived, for it is the sole authentic record of a multitude
of events highly important in a particularly interesting section of the history of England. Its importance as a product of biographical literature was first emphasized by Mandell Creighton, who insisted on the claim of Cavendish to be recognized as the earliest of the great English biographers, and an individual writer of charm and originality. He writes with simplicity and vividness, rarely yielding to the rhetoric which governed the ordinary prose of his age. 

He also knew Anne Boleyn when she was first a debutante at King Henry's court in one five two two . He was adamant that she remained a virgin until her marriage, despite Catholic rumours to the contrary. However, although he attested to her sexual morals, he never forgave her for her hatred of Cardinal Wolsey or her animosity towards the Pope.

'''Flemington''' is a Borough located in Hunterdon County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the borough had a total population of four , two zero one . It is the county seat of Hunterdon County.

On February one three , one nine three five a jury in Flemington found Bruno Richard Hauptmann guilty of the kidnapping and murder of Charles Lindbergh's baby boy.

Flemington is an independent municipality located entirely within (and completely surrounded by) Raritan Township and is located near the geographic center of the Township. In one seven five six , Samuel Fleming purchased part of this land, and built his home which still stands on Bonnell Street, and Fleming's Town was born.

 Geography 
Flemington is located at four zero  three zero ' three one  North, seven four  five one ' two nine  West ( four zero . five zero eight six five three , - seven four . eight five eight zero seven seven ).

According to the United States Census Bureau, the borough has a total area of two . eight km ( one . one mi ).  two . eight km ( one . one mi ) of it is land and none of the area is covered with water.

 Demographics 
As of the census of two zero zero zero , there are four , two zero two people, one , eight zero four households, and nine nine seven families residing in the borough. The population density is one , five one five . five km ( three , nine two seven . four mi ). There are one , eight seven six housing units at an average density of six seven six . nine km ( one , seven five four . two mi ). The racial makeup of the borough is eight seven . seven one % White, three . one nine % African American, zero . three one % Native American, three . one two % Asian, zero . one seven % Pacific Islander, three . one four % from other races, and two . three six % from two or more races.  one zero . nine eight % of the population are Hispanic or Latino of any race. Flemington is the home of the Mediatech Foundation, a community technology center. 

There are one , eight zero four households out of which two six . eight % have children under the age of one eight living with them, three eight . seven % are married couples living together, one one . seven % have a female householder with no husband present, and four four . seven % are non-families. three seven . seven % of all households are made up of individuals and one two . one % have someone living alone who is six five years of age or older. The average household size is two . two six and the average family size is three . zero zero .

In the borough the population is spread out with two two . two % under the age of one eight , eight . six % from one eight to two four , three six . nine % from two five to four four , two zero . two % from four five to six four , and one two . one % who are six five years of age or older. The median age is three five years. For every one zero zero females there are nine four . three males. For every one zero zero females age one eight and over, there are nine two . seven males.

The median income for a household in the borough is $ three nine , eight eight six , and the median income for a family is $ five one , five eight two . Males have a median income of $ three eight , five nine four versus $ three one , two five zero for females. The per capita income for the borough is $ two three , seven six nine .  six . nine % of the population and five . zero % of families are below the poverty line. Out of the total population, seven . five % of those under the age of one eight and three . zero % of those six five and older are living below the poverty line.

Flemington Circle
Aerial photo of Flemington Circle
'''Flemington Circle''' is the largest of three traffic circles in the environs of Flemington and sits just to the southeast of Flemington's historic downtown. U.S. Route two zero two and Route three one approach the circle separately from the north and continue south concurrent, and the circle is the eastern terminus of Route one two . It is one of only a handful of New Jersey's once-widespread traffic circles still extant according to its original design. Unlike most circles, traffic on US two zero two does not yield on entry; US two zero two , being a main four-lane divided highway, gets the right-of-way.

Two other traffic circles exist on Route one two just west of the Flemington Circle. Both are unnamed and handle a much smaller volume of traffic; the first one, at South Main Street (old Route three one ), is also in Flemington, and the other, at Flemington RoadRoute five two three (old Route one two ), is in Raritan Township.

 Government 
The Mayor of Flemington Borough is William Martin, Jr. Members of the Flemington Borough Council are Sandra Borucki, Donna Cocco, John Gorman, Robert Hauck, Mary Melfi and Joey Novick.
 Federal, state and county representation 
Flemington Borough is in the Seventh Congressional District and is part of New Jersey's two three rd Legislative District.

 

 



 Education 
Children grades K through eight attend the Flemington-Raritan Regional School District, which also serves children from the neighboring community of Raritan Township. The district consists of four K - four elementary schools  Barley Sheaf School ( four nine one students) - Flemington; Copper Hill School ( eight zero one students) - Ringoes; Francis A. Desmares School ( five four zero students) - Flemington; Robert Hunter School ( four nine nine students) - Flemington  Reading-Fleming Intermediate School in Flemington for grades five - six and J. P. Case Middle School ( one , one nine nine students) - Flemington for grades seven and eight . 

Students in grade nine - one two attend the Hunterdon Central Regional High School, part of the Hunterdon Central Regional High School District, which serves almost two , eight zero zero students in central Hunterdon County. Students from Delaware Township, East Amwell Township, Flemington Borough, Raritan Township and Readington Township attend Hunterdon Central Regional High School.

 History 
The land that comprises Flemington was originally the territory of the Lenni Lenape Native Americans, as was all of Hunterdon County. In one seven one two , as part of a land parcel of nine , one seven zero acres, the Flemington acreage was acquired by William Penn and Daniel Coxe.

The surrounding fertile farmland dictated that the beginnings of Flemington should be essentially agricultural. Early German and English settlers engaged in industries dependent on farm products. As time passed poultry and dairy farms superseded crops in agricultural importance.

In one seven eight five , Flemington was chosen as the County Seat of Hunterdon. Fire destroyed the old courthouse in one eight two six and the City of Lambertville made an attempt to have the Seat moved, to no avail. Flemington remained the County Seat and the Courthouse which stands today on Main Street was built.

In one eight five six , the Hunterdon County Agricultural society purchased four zero acres of land that would accommodate the people, exhibits and livestock for the County (Flemington) Fair. The purpose of this Fair was to promote competition between farmers, stock raisers and machinery manufacturers. In the year two zero zero three , the County Fair found a new home in Raritan Township.

By one nine eight zero , sixty-five percent of Flemington borough had been included on the New Jersey State Register of Historic Places and is now on the National Register of Historic Places.

Map of Franklin Township in Hunterdon County
'''Franklin Township''' is a Township located in Hunterdon County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the township had a total population of two , nine nine zero .

Franklin Township is centrally located in Hunterdon County. It was established in one eight four five when it was created from Kingwood Township. In its early days Franklin was a Quaker settlement. The most reliable records that are available about the early days of the Township are found in the minutes of the Friends' Meeting in Quakertown.

The Capoolong Creek, which runs through the community of Pittstown, was an attraction to early settlers and they soon established three of the oldest churches in present day Hunterdon: Thomas Episcopal, established in one seven two three , Bethlehem Presbyterian, organized in one seven three zero and the Quaker Church in one seven three three .

 Geography 
According to the United States Census Bureau, the township has a total area of five nine . four km ( two two . nine mi ).  five nine . three km ( two two . nine mi ) of it is land and zero . one km ( zero . zero four mi ) of it is water. The total area is zero . one seven % water.

'''Frenchtown''' is a Borough located in Hunterdon County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the borough had a total population of one , four eight eight .

Frenchtown Borough is located along the banks of the Delaware River. Various names have been applied to this settlement, after the many ferry operators residing on both sides of the river. Alexandria Ville and Frenchtown were the official names by which this community was known over the years. The Borough was formed from Alexandria Township in one eight six seven .

The first bridge across the Delaware at Frenchtown was built in one eight four four , and the town's prosperity increased as it became a gateway to Pennsylvania. A free Delaware River Joint Toll Bridge Commission bridge over the Delaware River connects Frenchtown to Uhlerstown, Tinicum Township, Bucks County, Pennsylvania. 

Frenchtown was the birthplace of Harvey Spencer Lewis.

 Map of Holland Township in Hunterdon County
'''Holland Township''' is a Township located in Hunterdon County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the township had a total population of five , one two four .

Holland Township is located in the northwestern part of Hunterdon County. The Delaware River forms its boundary with Pennsylvania and the Musconetcong River its boundary with Warren County. It was created from Alexandria Township in one eight seven four . In one eight seven six it was remerged with Alexandria Township and separated as a municipality of its own again in one eight seven nine .

The Volendam Windmill Museum is a living museum which demonstrates an authentic model of a mill driven by wind, used for grinding raw grain into flour. The sixty-foot structure is seven stories high with sail arms sixty-eight feet from tip to tip.

The Musconetcong Gorge Nature Preserve is a rugged undeveloped park under the direction of the Hunterdon County Parks and Recreational System. The Preserve is comprised of three seven nine acres of steeply wooded terrain overlooking the Musconetcong River. The gorge includes many spring-fed streams, a variety of plant species and wildlife. While the body of the area is a challenge to the seasoned hiker, a diverse trail system is being developed to provide accessibility for less-seasoned hikers.

Geography

 Map of Lambertville in Hunterdon County
'''Lambertville''' is a City located in Hunterdon County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the city had a total population of three , eight six eight .

Lambertville is located on the Delaware River in the southwestern portion of Hunterdon County. During the one seven zero zero 's, the City was named after various operators of ferries across the river to Pennsylvania, ultimately becoming known as Coryell's Ferry, after Emanuel Coryell who owned the Ferry. Coryell's Ferry was the western terminus of the New Jersey portion of the York Road (which is now known as U.S. Highway two zero two ) connecting New York City and Philadelphia. The City was named Lambertville in one eight one four when the post office was established and honored the Honorable John Lambert, a local resident, United States Senator and Governor of New Jersey.

The Delaware River and the Delaware and Raritan Canal were instrumental in the posterity of Lambertville. In June one eight three four , the opening of the canal was celebrated with a barge ride from Trenton to Lambertville. The canal's completion was not without hardship. four zero zero zero Irish immigrants were hired to dig the canal with pick and shovel. During the construction an epidemic of Cholera broke out and dozens of men were buried along the banks of the canal and the Delaware River.

 Geography 
Lambertville is located at four zero  two two ' four  North, seven four  five six ' three four  West ( four zero . three six seven eight eight one , - seven four . nine four two eight six zero ).

 Government 
Lambertville is governed by the Faulkner Act (Small Municipality) form of government. The Faulkner Act allows municipalities to adopt a Small Municipality form of government only for municipalities with a population of under one two , zero zero zero .

Voters select a Mayor and four Council members. Council members are elected at-large. Council serves three -year terms of office. The Mayor is elected by voters and serves a four -year term. 

The Mayor exercises executive power of the municipality. The Mayor presides over Council with voice and vote, but has no veto powers; Exercises executive power of the municipality; Appoints Council committees; Appoints municipal clerk, attorney, tax assessor, tax collector and the treasurer, all with Council confirmation; Council-elected mayor serves a term of one or three years, depending on whether terms are staggered or concurrent.

The Council exercises legislative power of the municipality and also approves Mayor's appointees for municipal clerk, attorney, tax assessor, tax collector and treasurer.

The Mayor of Lambertville is David M. DelVecchio. Members of the City Council are Council President 
John M. McManus, Cynthia L. Ege, Frank Kramer and Steven M. Stegman.

Lambertville City is in the Twelfth Congressional District and is part of New Jersey's two three rd Legislative District.

The Lambertville Public School serves students in grades kindergarten through grade six.

Students from Lambertville, Stockton and West Amwell Township attend South Hunterdon Regional High School.

Industry

The primary industry of Lambertville is tourism. On weekends the streets are crowded with tourists visiting the many restaurants, antique shops, art galleries, or just strolling along the river.

 Government 
 Local government 
Lebanon uses the Borough Form of Government. The Lebanon Borough Common Council consists of six Council Members and one Mayor elected at large.

'''Raritan Township''' is a Township located in Hunterdon County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the township had a total population of one nine , eight zero nine .

Raritan Township was formed from portions of the now-defunct Amwell Township. Raritan Township was also the former name of a community in Middlesex County, now known as Edison Township. 

 Geography 
According to the United States Census Bureau, the township has a total area of nine eight . two km ( three seven . nine mi ).  nine eight . zero km ( three seven . eight mi ) of it is land and zero . two km ( zero . one mi ) of it is water. The total area is zero . one eight % water.

Raritan Township borders East Amwell Township, Delaware Township, Franklin Township, Clinton Township, Readington Township. Flemington Borough is an independent municipality located entirely within Raritan Township. Raritan Township also borders Somerset County.

 Demographics 
As of the census two of two zero zero zero , there are one nine , eight zero nine people, six , nine three nine households, and five , three nine one families residing in the township. The population density is two zero two . one km ( five two three . five mi ). There are seven , zero nine four housing units at an average density of seven two . four km ( one eight seven . five mi ). The racial makeup of the township is nine three . two two % White, one . two three % African American, zero . zero nine % Native American, three . five zero % Asian, zero . zero one % Pacific Islander, zero . six eight % from other races, and one . two seven % from two or more races.  two . seven nine % of the population are Hispanic or Latino of any race.

There are six , nine three nine households out of which four three . zero % have children under the age of one eight living with them, six eight . two % are married couples living together, seven . zero % have a female householder with no husband present, and two two . three % are non-families. one eight . two % of all households are made up of individuals and five . six % have someone living alone who is six five years of age or older. The average household size is two . eight one and the average family size is three . two four .

Out of the total population, one . six % of those under the age of one eight and two . nine % of those six five and older are living below the poverty line.

 Government 
Raritan Township uses the Township form of government which is one of the oldest forms of government in New Jersey. The governing body is a township committee of five members who are elected for three-year staggered terms in partisan elections from the Township at large. There is an election of at least one member every year.

The Township Committee annually chooses one of the Committee to serve as mayor for that year. The mayor presides at Township Committee meetings and votes as a member of the Committee, but has no other special powers under the township form of government law. All legislative and executive powers, including the power of appointments, are exercised by the committee as a whole.

 Map of Readington Township in Hunterdon County
'''Readington Township''' is a Township located in the easternmost portion of Hunterdon County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the township had a total population of one five , eight zero three .

White House Station is a census-designated place and unincorporated area located within Readington Township.

Created by Royal Charter of King George II, Readings Township was formed July one five , one seven three zero . It was the first new township created after Hunterdon became a county. Containing almost forty-eight square miles, it remains the largest township in the County. Bounded on the north by the Lamington River and Rockaway Creek; to the east by Somerset County; to the south, the South Branch of the Raritan River; and to the west by the old West Jersey Society's line which crosses the Cushetunk Mountains.

 Geography 
According to the United States Census Bureau, the township has a total area of one two three . nine km ( four seven . eight mi ).  one two three . five km ( four seven . seven mi ) of it is land and zero . three km ( zero . one mi ) of it is water. The total area is zero . two five % water.

Readington Township borders Raritan Township, Clinton Township, and Tewksbury Township. Readington Township also borders Somerset County.

 Demographics 
As of the census two of two zero zero zero , there are one five , eight zero three people, five , six seven six households, and four , four one zero families residing in the township. The population density is one two seven . nine km ( three three one . four mi ). There are five , seven nine four housing units at an average density of four six . nine km ( one two one . five mi ). The racial makeup of the township is nine five . one four % White, zero . seven six % African American, zero . zero six % Native American, two . five six % Asian, zero . zero zero % Pacific Islander, zero . five three % from other races, and zero . nine four % from two or more races.  two . zero five % of the population are Hispanic or Latino of any race.

There are five , six seven six households out of which three seven . nine % have children under the age of one eight living with them, six nine . three % are married couples living together, six . one % have a female householder with no husband present, and two two . three % are non-families. one eight . two % of all households are made up of individuals and five . eight % have someone living alone who is six five years of age or older. The average household size is two . seven seven and the average family size is three . one eight .

In the township the population is spread out with two six . five % under the age of one eight , four . nine % from one eight to two four , three zero . six % from two five to four four , two eight . three % from four five to six four , and nine . eight % who are six five years of age or older. The median age is three nine years. For every one zero zero females there are nine seven . zero males. For every one zero zero females age one eight and over, there are nine three . seven males.

The median income for a household in the township is $ nine five , three five six , and the median income for a family is $ one zero six , three four three . Males have a median income of $ six six , seven seven eight versus $ four eight , three eight five for females. The per capita income for the township is $ four one , zero zero zero .  one . six % of the population and zero . seven % of families are below the poverty line. Out of the total population, one . four % of those under the age of one eight and one . eight % of those six five and older are living below the poverty line.

 Government 
Readington Township uses the Township form of government which is one of the oldest forms of government in New Jersey. The original Township Act of one seven nine eight incorporated one zero four townships. Designed to parallel the New England Township meeting, this form was modified continually throughout the one nine th century. The Township Act of one eight nine nine abolished the township meeting and replaced it with a township committee with all municipal powers. This act, with a handful of amendments, served until it was repealed by the Township Act of one nine eight nine , which cleared up many ambiguities of the previous law.

Under the current township government laws, the township committee remains the backbone of the municipality's government. Voters elect, at-large, the township committee comprising of five members. The elections are partisan and the committee members serve staggered three-year terms. The Township Committee elects the mayor and deputy mayor each January from its members for a one-year term. The Mayor serves as chair of the Township Committee and has the powers vested in the mayor's office by general law.

Members of the Readington Township Committee are Mayor Frank L. Gatti (term ends December two zero zero five ), Deputy Mayor Gerard J. Shamey ( two zero zero seven ), Julia C. Allen ( two zero zero five ), Tom Auriemma ( two zero zero six ) and Beatrice Muir ( two zero zero six ).
 Federal, state and county representation 
Readington Township is in the Seventh Congressional District and is part of New Jersey's two three rd Legislative District.

 

 



 Education 
The Readington Township Public Schools serve students in grades kindergarten through grade eight. Schools in the district are Whitehouse School (K- two ), Three Bridges School (K- two ), Holland Brook School ( three - five ) and Readington Middle School ( six - eight ).

Students in grade nine - one two attend the Hunterdon Central High School, part of the Hunterdon Central Regional High School District, which serves almost two , eight zero zero students in central Hunterdon County. Students from Delaware Township, East Amwell Township, Flemington Borough, Raritan Township and Readington Township attend Hunterdon Central High School.

 Business 
Readington Township is home to the Global Headquarters of Merck, one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in the country. Readington is also close to Interstate seven eight , Princeton, Bridgewater Township and other centers for business in central New Jersey.

 Map of Stockton in Hunterdon County
'''Stockton''' is a Borough located in Hunterdon County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the borough had a total population of five six zero .

Stockton, located along the Delaware River north of Lambertville, was first known as Reading Ferry and subsequently Howell's Ferry. With the arrival of the railroad, the name was changed to Centre Bridge Station which corresponded to the post office and hamlet on the Pennsylvania side of the river. With the establishment of its own post office in one eight five one , the village was renamed Stockton. The Borough was incorporated in one eight nine eight , having been separated from Delaware Township.

The tiny town remains today as it was in the eighteenth century. for all its small size and charm, the town is presided over by an old inn. The Stockton Inn (formally known as Colligan's Stockton Inn), established in one seven one zero , is the inn that was immortalized by Richard Rodgers in the song There's a small hotel with a wishing well , sung in the Broadway play ''On Your Toes''. The inn was first built as a private residence and is believed to have been converted in one eight three two .

The Delaware River Mill Society was formed to preserve and promote the buildings and site known as the Prallsville Mills. John Prall, Jr., became the owner of the site in one seven nine four and with his settlement the area became known as Prallsville.

 Geography 
Stockton is located at four zero  two four ' two four  North, seven four  five eight ' three nine  West ( four zero . four zero six seven zero one , - seven four . nine seven seven five four six ).

 U.S. M six zero Patton tank. The rear drive sprocket and return rollers holding up the track are clearly seen.
'''Caterpillar tracks''' are large (modular) tracks used on tanks, construction equipment and certain other off-road vehicles. Unlike the Kegresse tracks which use a flexible belt, caterpillar tracks are made of a number of rigid units that are joined to each other. The tracks help the vehicle to distribute its weight more evenly over a larger surface area than wheels can, keeping it from sinking in areas where wheeled vehicles of the same weight would sink. For instance, the ground pressure of a car is equal to the pressure of the air in the tires, perhaps three zero psi ( two zero seven kPa), whereas the seventy-tonne M one Abrams tank has a ground pressure of just over one five psi ( one zero three kPa). 

 History 
A crude caterpillar track was designed in one seven seven zero by Richard Edgeworth. The British polymath Sir George Cayley patented a caterpillar track, which he called a universal railway (The Mechanics' Magazine, two eight January one eight two six ). In one eight three seven , a Russian inventor Dmitry Zagryazhsky designed a carriage with mobile tracks which he patented that same year. However, due to a lack of funds he was unable to build a working prototype. As a result his patent was voided in one eight three nine . Steam powered tractors using a form of caterpillar track were reported in use with the Western Alliance during the Crimean War in the one eight five zero s.

An effective caterpillar track was invented and implemented by Alvin Lombard, for the Lombard steam log hauler. He was granted a patent in one nine zero one . He built the first steam-powered log hauler at the Waterville Iron Works in Waterville, Maine the same year. In all, eighty-three Lombard steam log haulers are known to have been built up to one nine one seven when production switched entirely to internal combustion engine powered machines ending with a Fairbanks diesel powered unit in one nine three four , yet undoubtedly Lombard was the first commercial manufacturer of the crawler tractor. In addition, there may have been up to twice as many Phoenix Centipeed versions of the steam log hauler built under license from Lombard, with vertical instead of horizontal cylinders. In one nine zero three , the founder of the Holt Manufacturing, Benjamin Holt, paid Lombard $ six zero , zero zero zero so they could produce vehicles under his patent. Their seems to have been an agreement made after Lombard travelled out to CA, but some discrepancy as to how this matter was resolved when previous track patents were studied. Popularly, everyone claimed to have been inspired by the dog tread mill once used on farms to power the butter churn, etc. to invent the crawler on their own, and the more recent the history, the earlier this date of invention seems to get.

At about the same time a British agricultural company Hornsby based in Grantham, in the United Kingdom developed a caterpillar track which was patented in one nine zero five . The design differed from modern tracks in that it flexed in only one direction with the effect that the links locked together to form a solid rail on which the road wheels ran. Hornsby's tracked vehicles were used as artillery tractors by the British Army from one nine zero six . Their patent was also purchased by Holt. The Hornsby tractors featured the track-steer clutch arrangement which is the basis of the modern crawler operation, and some say an observing British soldier quipped that it crawled like a caterpillar . What is known is that caterpillar became a generic term for this type of machine. The word was shrewdly trademarked and defended by Holt).

Following a merger and name change, The Holt Manufacturing Company became the Caterpillar Tractor Company in one nine two five . Caterpillar tracks have since revolutionized construction vehicles and land warfare. Track systems have been developed and improved during the years. The first tanks to be fielded were developed from Holt tractors which were already in use towing artillery over the difficult terrain of the Western Front of the First World War. 

Perhaps the oldest implementation of something like tracks is to be found in theories of prehistoric erection of large stone monuments, when megaliths may have been slid atop rounded wooden logs. The logs were grooved near their ends to be held in alignment and rotation by belts out past the edge of the megalith and lubricated by some means, probably organic. The logs are carried from the back of the procession to the front in an endless chain, like caterpillar track. Attempts by experimental archaeologists to reconstruct these methods have met with varying success. The system is a pre-cursor to development of the axle which keep a rotating cylinder fixed to its cargo.

The Israeli Defence Forces have developed an improved suspension system, called ''Mazkum   ''(or  for short), which enables greater mobility than regular tracks. The ''Mazkum'' is installed on the Israeli Merkava tank which helps improve mobility and speed, some of the Israeli patents were sold to Caterpillar Tractor.

 Engineering 
 Soviet T- five five tank with slack track and rear drive sprocket.

Modern tracks are built from modular chain links which compose together a closed chain. These chain links are often broad and made of alloy steel. The links are jointed by a hinge. This allows the track to be flexible and maintain its elliptical shape.

The vehicle's weight is suspended from a number of road wheels, or bogies . Road wheels are typically mounted on some form of suspension to cushion the ride over rough ground. Suspension design is a major area of development; early designs offered only a few inches of travel using springs, whereas modern hydro-pneumatic systems allow several feet of travel and include shock absorbers.

Tracks are moved by a toothed drive wheel, or ''drive sprocket'', driven by the motor and engaging with holes in the track links to drive the track. The drive wheel is typically mounted well above the contact area on the ground, allowing it to be fixed in position. Placing a suspension on the driving wheel is possible, but is mechanically more complicated. A non-powered wheel, an ''idler'', is placed at the opposite end of the track, primarily to angle the front (or rear) of the track to allow it to climb over obstacles. Some track arrangements use ''return rollers'' to keep the top of the track running straight between the drive sprocket and idler. Others allow the track to droop and run along the tops of large road wheels, called ''slack track''.

Tracked vehicles have better mobility than pneumatic tires over rough terrain. They smooth out the bumps and glide over small obstacles; riding in a fast tracked vehicle feels like riding in a boat over heavy swells. Tracks are tougher than tires since they cannot be punctured or torn. Tracks are much less likely to get stuck in soft ground, mud, or snow, since they distribute the weight of the vehicle over a larger contact area, decreasing its ground pressure. Bulldozers, which are most often tracked, uses this attribute to rescue other vehicles (such as wheel loaders) which have become stuck in or sunk into the ground. 

The disadvantages of tracks are lower top speed and the damage that they cause to what passes beneath them: they can severely damage lawns, farm fields, and even asphalt pavement. Prolonged use places enormous strain on the drive transmission and the mechanics of the tracks, which must be overhauled or replaced regularly. It is common to see tracked vehicles such as bulldozers or tanks transported long distances by a wheeled carrier such as a semitrailer or train, though technological advances have made this practice less common among tracked military vehicles than it once was.

A recent innovation by Caterpillar is a rubber track tractor for agricultural use, such as the Cat Challenger Tractor, MT seven zero zero and MT eight zero zero series. Instead of a track made of linked steel plates, it uses a reinforced rubber belt with chevron treads for improved traction and reduced soil compaction. Having a rubber belt also means that the vehicle can relocate itself on public roads without damaging pavement.

West Amwell Township was originally part of Amwell Township, which was formed in one seven zero eight when Hunterdon County was still part of Burlington County.  Government 
West Amwell Township uses the Township form of government which is one of the oldest forms of government in New Jersey. The governing body is a township committee of three members who are elected for three-year staggered terms in partisan elections from the Township at large. 

The Township Committee annually chooses one of the Committee to serve as mayor for that year. The mayor presides at Township Committee meetings and votes as a member of the Committee, but has no other special powers under the township form of government law. All legislative and executive powers, including the power of appointments, are exercised by the committee as a whole.

This portion of one three zero is now becoming more congested since many new businesses (such as Wal-Mart) are being built. East Windsor Township houses the New Jersey Turnpike's Exit eight . Exit eight is slowly becoming busier as development sets foot in East Windsor. At the present time, there has been an announcement that the Turnpike will be widened from three lanes to a five -lane turnpike. Such an expansion can be assumed since Route one three three has extra space on the outer edges of the Turnpike.

In the late one nine nine zero 's, the Hightstown Bypass (Route one three three ) was constructed. It starts at County Route five seven one and terminates at three three . The entire highway is in East Windsor; there is a half-diamond interchange with One Mile Road, and a three-quarter cloverleaf with U.S. Route one three zero . Both ends of the bypass are handled with traffic signals instead of grade seperated interchanges. Despite the bypass being built, the New Jersey Turnpike Authority has not made any comment on building a new exit with the Turnpike. The new interchange (if built) would provide a direct connection between the one three three highway and the Turnpike; it would also make it easier for some motorists to travel to Princeton. 

 Government 
 Local government 
East Windsor Township has a Council-Manager form of government as provided under the Faulkner Act. The Council is made up of seven members elected at large for four-year staggered terms. Elections for Council are held in November of every other year.

Members of the East Windsor Township Council are Mayor Janice S. Mironov, Deputy Mayor Hector Duke, Walter T. Daniels, Marc Lippman, Alan Rosenberg, Perry M. Shapiro and Marsha Weinstein.
 Federal, state and county representation 
East Windsor Township is in the Fourth Congressional District and is part of New Jersey's one two th Legislative District.

 

 



 Education 
Students in Kindergarten through one two th grade attend the East Windsor Regional School District, a comprehensive public school district serving students from East Windsor Township and Hightstown Borough, along with students in grades seven - one two from Roosevelt Borough as part of a sending receiving relationship.

The distrcit has four K- five elementary schools 
 Walter C. Black Elementary School with five eight one students, Perry L. Drew Elementary School with six nine two students, Ethel McKnight Elementary School with five seven two students, Grace N. Rogers Elementary School with five zero two students

'''Ewing Township''' is a Township located in Mercer County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the township had a total population of three five , seven zero seven .

Although Ewing Township was officially established in one eight three four , the history of the region ranges back thousands of years. The earliest inhabitants of the land area today known as Ewing Township were the Lenni Lenape Native Americans. These migratory people ranged throughout New Jersey along the banks of the Delaware River, and the Township's many creeks provided rich natural resources for hunting, fishing, pottery-making, and simple farming.

When the region was first settled by European colonists around one six nine nine , it was part of Hopewell Township, and continued under that name until the City of Trenton was established in one seven one nine . From one seven one nine until one eight three four , the area was named Trenton Township. On February two two , one eight three four , the name was changed from Trenton Township to Ewing Township in honor of Charles Ewing, who was posthumously honored for his work as Chief Justice of the New Jersey Supreme Court from one eight two four - one eight three two .

 Geography 
Ewing is located at four zero  one five ' three six  North, seven four  four seven ' two zero  West ( four zero . two five nine nine five eight , - seven four . seven eight eight eight four two ).

According to the United States Census Bureau, the township has a total area of four zero . four km ( one five . six mi ).  three nine . seven km ( one five . three mi ) of it is land and zero . seven km ( zero . three mi ) of it is water, mostly consisting of the Delaware River. The total area is one . seven three % water.

Ewing Township shares land borders with Hopewell Township, Lawrence Township, and the City of Trenton, all in New Jersey; the Delaware River separates Ewing from Lower Makefield Township and Yardley Borough, both in Pennsylvania.

 Demographics 
As of the census of two zero zero zero , there are three five , seven zero seven people, one two , five five one households, and eight , two zero eight families residing in the township. The population density is eight nine nine . three km ( two , three two eight . six mi ). There are one two , nine two four housing units at an average density of three two five . five km ( eight four two . eight mi ). The racial makeup of the township is six nine . zero two % White, two four . eight two % African American, zero . one five % Native American, two . two seven % Asian, zero . zero six % Pacific Islander, one . eight three % from other races, and one . eight four % from two or more races.  four . four four % of the population are Hispanic or Latino of any race.

There are one two , five five one households out of which two five . three % have children under the age of one eight living with them, four nine . seven % are married couples living together, one two . two % have a female householder with no husband present, and three four . six % are non-families. two seven . seven % of all households are made up of individuals and one two . one % have someone living alone who is six five years of age or older. The average household size is two . four five and the average family size is three . zero zero .

In the township the population is spread out with one eight . zero % under the age of one eight , one seven . three % from one eight to two four , two six . eight % from two five to four four , two two . one % from four five to six four , and one five . eight % who are six five years of age or older. The median age is three seven years. For every one zero zero females there are nine three . zero males. For every one zero zero females age one eight and over, there are nine zero . zero males.

The median income for a household in the township is $ five seven , two seven four , and the median income for a family is $ six seven , six one eight . Males have a median income of $ four four , five three one versus $ three five , eight four four for females. The per capita income for the township is $ two four , two six eight .  six . four % of the population and three . three % of families are below the poverty line. Out of the total population, five . four % of those under the age of one eight and seven . one % of those six five and older are living below the poverty line.

 Township Layout 
Ewing Township was originally farmland punctuated by hamlets, including Ewingville, West Trenton, and Wilburtha. Since the beginning of the two zero th Century, the township has developed as a suburb of Trenton. The sections near the city border are distinctly urban, but most of the township is suburban residential development. The main commercial district extends along North Olden Avenue Extension (County Route six two two ), originally constructed to connect north Trenton residences with the now-closed General Motors plant. Ewing Township is also the location of the New Jersey State Police headquarters, the New Jersey State Prison Farm, the New Jersey Department of Transportation headquarters, and Trenton-Mercer Airport (KTTN), the location of Trenton, New Jersey's weather observations.

 Government 
 Local government 
Ewing Township is governed under a Mayor-Council, under the Faulkner Act. The Governing Body of the township consists of five Council members and a Mayor, all of whom are elected by the residents of the community. The Mayor is elected to a four-year term. Members of the Council are elected to staggered four-year terms.

The Mayor of Ewing Township is Wendell Pribila. Members of the Ewing Township Council are Council President Kathy Wollert, Council Vice President Don Apai, Joe Murphy, Bert Steinmann and Les Summiel.
 Federal, state and county representation 
Ewing Township is in the Twelfth Congressional District and is part of New Jersey's one five th Legislative District.

 

 



 Education 
The Ewing Township Board of Education oversees the Ewing Public Schools. At present, the district includes three elementary schools with kindergarten and grades one through five ( Lore, Antheil, and Parkway), one middle school with grades six through eight ( Fisher), and one high school with grades nine through one two (Ewing High School). An adult school is also administered.

The College of New Jersey (formerly Trenton State College) is located within the Ewingville section of the township.

 Transportation 
Ewing Township is traversed by multiple main roadways, as well as by a passenger rail line and is the location of an airport. 

Route two nine (Daniel Bray Highway and River Road) extends north-south along the western edge of the township, along the Delaware River. The southern section, Daniel Bray Highway, is a five five mph ( nine zero kmh), divided four -lane facility with at-grade intersections and traffic lights, and was constructed in the one nine five zero s. The northern section, River Road, is a four five mph ( seven zero kmh), undivided two -lane facility whose construction as a state highway dates from the one nine three zero s. NJ two nine connects southwards to Trenton, New Jersey, and northwards to Lambertville and Frenchtown. 

Route three one (Pennington Road) extends north-south towards the eastern side of the township. It is a three five - four five mph ( six zero - seven zero kmh), undivided four -lane facility whose construction as a state highway also dates to the one nine three zero s. It once also carried a trolley line, but it has long since been removed. It was once proposed to be bypassed by a freeway, but this plan has since been cancelled. NJ three one also connects south to Trenton, and connects north to Pennington, Flemington, and Clinton. 

U.S. Route two zero six (Princeton Avenue) skirts the southeastern section of the township. It is a two five mph ( four zero kmh), undivided four -lane facility. Although part of US two zero six , it was not constructed and is not maintained by the state. US two zero six also connects south to Trenton, and connects north to Princeton and Somerville.

Interstate nine five (the Scudder Falls Expressway and Bridge) crosses the northwestern section of the township. It is a five five - six five mph ( nine zero - one zero zero kmh), four - six lane divided freeway facility. It was constructed as a four -lane facility in the one nine six zero s, and widened to six lanes in the one nine nine zero s, with the exception of the Scudder Falls Bridge over the Delaware River. It connects south with Philadelphia, Pennsylvania and connects north to U.S. one , where this branch of Interstate nine five ends. It becomes Interstate two nine five and turns south, forcing travellers to utilize either U.S. one or Interstate one nine five and the New Jersey Turnpike to reach the next major destination northwards, New York City. The Ewing portion of Interstate nine five will eventually be redesignated as Interstate two nine five when a direct interchange between Interstate nine five in Pennsylvania and the Pennsylvania Turnpike is completed, re-routing Interstate nine five onto the New Jersey Turnpike at Exit six . 

Ewing Township also boasts a commuter rail facility, West Trenton Station, at the terminus of SEPTA's R three Regional Rail line. This facility mainly serves commuter traffic to and from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The West Trenton Railyard, located just north of the West Trenton Station, serves freight trains daily as they travel along the Conrail-operated (ex-Reading Railroad) branch between Somerville and Philadelphia.

Ewing Township is also the site of the Trenton-Mercer Airport (TTN). This facility is the site of limited commercial flights to various east coast locations, as well as a substantial public recreational airport.

Ewing Township is also traversed by the Delaware & Raritan Canal near the Delaware River. Originally important to commerce and trade, the advent of railroads caused the canal's commercial demise. The strip of land along the canal is currently a state park.

 '''Georgiana Cavendish, Duchess of Devonshire''' (June seven , one seven five seven - March three zero , one eight zero six ), born '''Lady Georgiana Spencer''', was the first wife of William Cavendish, five th Duke of Devonshire and mother of William George Spencer Cavendish, six th Duke of Devonshire. Her father, John, one st Earl Spencer, was a great-grandson of John Churchill, one st Duke of Marlborough. Her niece was Lady Caroline Lamb. Among her descendants are the present Duke of Devonshire (via her granddaughter).

Georgiana was a celebrated beauty and a socialite who gathered around her a large circle of literary and political figures -- a ''salon''. She was also an active political campaigner in an age when women's suffrage was still over a century away. Both the Spencers and the Cavendishes were Whigs. Georgiana campaigned for the Whigs -- particularly for a distant cousin, Charles James Fox -- at a time when the King (George III) and his Ministers had more direct influence over the House of Commons, principally through their power of patronage. During the one seven eight four general election, the Duchess was rumored to have traded kisses for votes in favor of Fox.

Georgiana married the incumbent Duke on June six , one seven seven four . The marriage was a brilliant but unhappy one, with the couple mismatched by temperament. The young Duchess's early childlessness was also a matter of concern when aristocratic wives were valued as much for their fertility as for their dowries and connections. She gave birth to two daughters, before the much-awaited heir (and only) son was born. This son William George Spencer Cavendish, six th Duke of Devonshire died unmarried in one eight five eight ; her daughters were Georgiana Cavendish ( one seven eight three - one eight five eight ), who married George Howard ( one seven seven three - one eight four four ), six th Earl of Carlisle, and Harriet Cavendish ( one seven eight five - one eight six two ), who married Granville Leveson-Gower, one st Earl Granville.

It was Georgiana who introduced the Duke to his mistress and second wife-to-be, Lady Elizabeth Foster.  Bess was Georgiana's best friend, and she tolerated the ''menage-a-trois'' for many years. Georgiana herself formed a relationship with Charles Grey, two nd Earl Grey, by whom she had a daughter (an ancestor of Sarah, Duchess of York). Lady Elizabeth Foster had two children by the Duke -- a son and daughter.  When the Duchess died, her husband married Bess Foster -- and promptly set up a new mistress. At his death, his son by his first wife Georgiana became six th Duke but died unmarried. He was succeeded by a first cousin once removed William Cavendish, seven th Duke of Devonshire ( one eight zero eight - one eight nine one ), who was widower of the six th Duke's niece and Georgiana's granddaughter Lady Blanche Howard.

Georgiana was famous not only for her marital arrangements, her beauty and sense of style, her political campaigning, but also for her love of gambling. She was reported to have died deeply in debt, even though her own family the Spencers and her husband's family the Cavendishes were immensely wealthy.

During her years in the public eye, Georgiana was painted by Thomas Gainsborough and Joshua Reynolds. Gainsborough's famous painting of her in a large French hat was lost for many years. 

Another well-known woman from the same family as Georgiana was Diana, Princess of Wales (born Lady Diana Spencer), who was descended from Georgiana's brother, the two nd Earl Spencer.

'''Hamilton Township''' is a Township located in Mercer County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the township had a total population of eight seven , one zero nine . The township is located right next to the city of Trenton, the capital of New Jersey. Hamilton Township is governed under the Faulkner Act (Mayor-Council) system of municipal government.

Hamilton hosts one of the largest recreational parks in the state, and borders another. Veterans Park is three five zero acres and is housed entirely in the township. Mercer County Park borders the township to the North and encompasses two , five zero zero acres of land that was shared from Hamilton Township along with neighboring Lawrence Township and West Windsor Township. This park contains one of the largest man-made lakes in the state, and was built as a result of a Princeton University grant as a place for the University's crew team to practice and compete.

 Geography 
According to the United States Census Bureau, the township has a total area of one zero four . six km ( four zero . four mi ).  one zero two . two km ( three nine . five mi ) of it is land and two . four km ( zero . nine mi ) of it is water. The total area is two . two eight % water.

Hamilton Township borders Trenton, Lawrence Township, West Windsor Township, Washington Township, Bordentown Township, Chesterfield Township, Upper Freehold Township, and the Delaware River.

Mercerville-Hamilton Square, White Horse and Yardville-Groveville are all census-designated places and unincorporated areas located within Hamilton Township.

 Demographics 
As of the census two of two zero zero zero , there are eight seven , one zero nine people, three three , five two three households, and two three , six six seven families residing in the township. The population density is eight five two . five km ( two , two zero eight . zero mi ). There are three four , five three five housing units at an average density of three three eight . zero km ( eight seven five . four mi ). The racial makeup of the township is eight five . one five % White, eight . one six % African American, zero . one four % Native American, two . five six % Asian, zero . zero four % Pacific Islander, two . one nine % from other races, and one . seven six % from two or more races.  five . one three % of the population are Hispanic or Latino of any race.

There are three three , five two three households out of which three one . two % have children under the age of one eight living with them, five five . three % are married couples living together, one one . five % have a female householder with no husband present, and two nine . four % are non-families. two four . five % of all households are made up of individuals and one zero . eight % have someone living alone who is six five years of age or older. The average household size is two . five eight and the average family size is three . one zero .

In the township the population is spread out with two three . two % under the age of one eight , seven . zero % from one eight to two four , two nine . nine % from two five to four four , two four . two % from four five to six four , and one five . six % who are six five years of age or older. The median age is three nine years. For every one zero zero females there are nine one . one males. For every one zero zero females age one eight and over, there are eight seven . zero males.

The median income for a household in the township is $ five seven , one one zero , and the median income for a family is $ six six , nine eight six . Males have a median income of $ four six , three six zero versus $ three three , six seven three for females. The per capita income for the township is $ two five , four four one .  four . two % of the population and two . eight % of families are below the poverty line. Out of the total population, five . four % of those under the age of one eight and five . six % of those six five and older are living below the poverty line.

As of late two zero zero five , much of the new residential development in Hamilton has been geared to accommodating the aging baby boomer generation. Retirement communities and assisted-living facilities outpace that of traditional residential communities. Such construction has been spurred by several factors. The first being that school budgets have always been kept low. Hamilton voters have a proven track record for vetoing school budgets in their yearly elections to keep taxes low. Another reason is the ramping up of Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital. The hospital is now a highly respected source of care in the state. It is also situated next to where most of the undeveloped land in the township used to be.

 Transportation 
New Jersey's eighth-largest municipality, Hamilton Township is less than an hour's ride from New York City, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania and the Jersey Shore. With over nine zero , zero zero zero residents and four zero -square miles of land, it is blessed with a rich mix of neighborhoods. With a bustling, modern train station and access to the New Jersey Turnpike, Interstate two nine five , Interstate one nine five , U.S. Route one three zero , U.S. Route two zero six , Route three three and U.S. Route one , it is a transportation hub.

With the addition of the Hamilton train station on transportation provider New Jersey Transit's Northeast Corridor Line, the township has attracted more New York City-based commuters to the area.

Located in Hamilton Township is the neighborhood of White Horse, which includes the White Horse Circle, a traffic circle on U.S. Route two zero six .

 Government 
 Local government 
The Mayor of Hamilton Township is Glen D. Gilmore (D). Members of the Township Council are Council President Thomas Goodwin (R) (elected two zero zero five ), Council Vice President Dave Kenny (R) (elected two zero zero five ), Dennis A. Pone (R) (elected two zero zero five ), Edward Pattik (D), and Shannon Cenci (D).

The Current Council was taken over in the majority by Republicans in a full sweep for three members, Dennis Pone, Dave Kenny, and Thomas Goodwin, on November two , two zero zero five .

 Federal, state and county representation 
Hamilton Township is in the Fourth Congressional District and is part of New Jersey's one four th Legislative District.

Hopewell was the town nearest to the estate owned by Charles Lindbergh and Anne Morrow Lindbergh. Their firstborn son, Charles Augustus Lindbergh III, was found dead near the town. See Lindbergh kidnapping for more information about the incident involving the Lindbergh child.

Hopewell Township, the much larger municipality in which Hopewell Borough is located, includes the land along the east side of the Delaware River to which George Washington and the Continental Army crossed from Pennsylannia. Today, Washington Crossing State Park commemorates this important milestone in American history.

'''Hopewell Township''' is a Township located in Mercer County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the township had a total population of one six , one zero five .

 Geography

'''Lawrence Township''' is a Township located in Mercer County, New Jersey. As of the United States two zero zero zero Census, the township had a total population of two nine , one five nine .

 Geography 
According to the United States Census Bureau, the township has a total area of five seven . four km ( two two . two mi ).  five seven . three km ( two two . one mi ) of it is land and zero . one km ( zero . zero four mi ) of it is water. The total area is zero . one eight % water.

Lawrence Township is commonly referred to as Lawrenceville by area residents. Lawrenceville is a census-designated place and unincorporated area located within Lawrence Township. The Post Office instructs many Lawrence Township residents to use Lawrenceville in their mailing address.

Lawrence Township is located in central Mercer County north of the City of Trenton, which is the county seat and capital of New Jersey. Ewing and Hopewell Townships lie to the west of Lawrence, Princeton and West Windsor Townships to the north and east, and Hamilton Township to the east and south. Lawrence is located midway between New York City and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, approximately five four and three three miles distant, respectively. 

 Demographics 
As of the census two of two zero zero zero , there are two nine , one five nine people, one zero , seven nine seven households, and seven , two three three families residing in the township. There are one zero , seven nine seven households out of which three one . four % have children under the age of one eight living with them, five three . nine % are married couples living together, one zero . five % have a female householder with no husband present, and three three . zero % are non-families. two six . eight % of all households are made up of individuals and nine . seven % have someone living alone who is six five years of age or older. The average household size is two . four nine and the average family size is three . zero five .

In the township the population is spread out with two one . seven % under the age of one eight , one two . four % from one eight to two four , two nine . four % from two five to four four , two three . zero % from four five to six four , and one three . six % who are six five years of age or older. The median age is three seven years. For every one zero zero females there are eight eight . zero males. For every one zero zero females age one eight and over, there are eight four . four males.
